name: Incident Response Conventions
description: This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on incident response so output stays consistent and easy to review.
content:
This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on incident response so output stays consistent and easy to review.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When multiple incident response strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
2. Surface known limitations of a chosen incident response approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
3. Check that incident response terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
4. Prefer explicit, readable incident response solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
5. Keep incident response changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
6. When incident response decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
7. Before starting incident response work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
8. When incident response guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
9. Re-check edge cases relevant to incident response (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
10. State assumptions about incident response explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
11. Measure before optimizing any incident response bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of incident response correctness.
- Do not apply generic incident response advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting incident response assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not silently drop incident response edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for incident response, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
